title: Urban Water Use in the CONUS: Evolution From Deterministic to Chaotic Dynamics
content:
Abstract

Historical records show that urban water use in the Contiguous United States has evolved from early steady levels (pre-1960s), to rapid growth (1970s–1980s), and to a recent phase marked by gradual decline, but along with significant inter-annual variability (post-1980s). Past studies have relied on statistical or machine learning models to link water use with climatic drivers such as precipitation, temperature, and humidity; and socioeconomic drivers such as population, income, and employment. However, they often struggle with capturing non-stationary relationships and dynamic coupling between climatic and socioeconomic drivers, and therefore, miss effective water use prediction. This study analyzes urban water use in the context of a coupled natural-human system (CNHS). Using more than 30 years of annual records from 10 U.S. cities, analysis of the maximal Lyapunov exponents reveals that water use in cities such as San Antonio, TX; Provo, UT; Oklahoma City, OK; and Tampa, FL shows chaotic dynamics with non-standard, highly unpredictable dynamical behavior. Meanwhile, water use in cities such as New York, NY; Sacramento, CA; and Long Beach, CA retains more deterministic characteristics. Furthermore, it is found that a climatic driver, Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI), emerges as the dominant source of this chaotic behavior. Building on this finding, we propose a gain-scheduling system dynamics framework that partitions the nonlinear system into linear subsystems under specified PDSI conditions. This approach balances interpretability with predictive power, providing a tool for predicting water use with complex dynamics and highlighting critical implications for urban water planning under increasing climatic fluctuation.
